title: Selecting Elements with jQuery
summary: Shows that $() takes any CSS selector and replaces both querySelector and querySelectorAll, returning a jQuery object whether one or many elements match.

concepts.heading: Selecting with $()
points: $("h1") replaces document.querySelector("h1"); the dollar sign stands for jQuery.

The argument is a standard CSS selector string: type selectors ("h1"), class selectors (".title"), id selectors ("#header"), combinators such as descendant ("#header h1") and compound selectors ("h1.title"). Selector syntax is unchanged from CSS.
CSS selectors were chosen because they are flexible and can be as specific as needed.

concepts.heading: One call for one or many
points: In vanilla JS you must choose querySelector (first match) or querySelectorAll (all matches). jQuery has a single form, so $("button") grabs all buttons.
Methods called on the result apply to every matched element, so no explicit loop is needed.
(Extra) The returned value is a jQuery object (array-like wrapper), not a raw DOM node; logging it in the console shows a list of matches. Use $("h1")[0] or .get(0) to reach the raw element.

code_examples.caption: Selecting in jQuery and logging the results (matches the reference repo)
code_examples.code:
console.log($("h1"));
console.log($("button"));   // all five buttons in one object

pitfalls: The result is a jQuery object, not a DOM element: DOM properties like .style or .innerText are not available directly on it; use jQuery methods instead.
Selecting is silent when nothing matches: you get an empty object rather than an error.

gaps_and_ideas: A jQuery selectors lesson: starter HTML with an h1, class and id elements and five buttons. Tasks: log $() with a tag, class and id selector; compare .length to querySelectorAll; find which of the console objects is a jQuery object. Demo: type a selector and highlight the matches live.
